questions.prompt: Why do AI language models hallucinate?

options.text: They are programmed to lie when they don't know.
options.explanation: There is no intent. The model produces likely-sounding text, and that is sometimes false.

options.text: They generate plausible-sounding text rather than looking up verified facts, so gaps get filled with confident inventions.
options.explanation: Correct. Predicting likely text is the core mechanism, which is why grounding in real sources helps so much.

options.text: Only old or free models hallucinate.
options.explanation: All current models can hallucinate. Better models do it less, but never zero.

options.text: Because the internet is full of mistakes, and that's the only cause.
options.explanation: Bad training data can contribute, but models also invent things that appear nowhere in their training data.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce hallucinations? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Giving the model the source documents and telling it to answer only from them
options.explanation: Yes. This is called grounding, and it is the most effective single fix.

options.text: Telling it that it may answer 'Not stated in the documents'
options.explanation: Yes. Permission not to know removes the pressure to invent an answer.

options.text: Asking it to quote the sentence it relied on
options.explanation: Yes. Quoted evidence lets a human check the answer in seconds.

options.text: Telling it to sound more confident
options.explanation: No. Confidence of tone has no link to accuracy, and this makes errors harder to spot.

questions.scenario: An electrician wants AI to write the hazards and controls section of the RAMS for every job, and send it straight to the main contractor.
questions.prompt: Using the traffic-light check, what do you advise?

options.text: Green: AI drafts, a quick glance is enough.
options.explanation: A safety document is never green. Mistakes can injure people.

options.text: Amber: AI drafts and the office manager approves.
options.explanation: Better, but the office manager may not be competent to judge electrical hazards. This needs a competent person.

options.text: Red: AI can help with formatting and plain English, but a competent person must own and approve the content, and nothing goes out automatically.
options.explanation: Correct. Safety content is red: a competent person owns it, with AI assisting at most.

options.text: AI should never be used anywhere near a RAMS document.
options.explanation: Overly strict. AI can usefully help format and clarify content a competent person has decided.

questions.prompt: Which task is AI generally BEST suited to?

options.text: Calculating the VAT total on a 40-line quote
options.explanation: Totals and VAT belong in a spreadsheet or accounting system. AI can draft the wording around them.

options.text: Summarising a 30-email thread with a client into the key decisions and open questions
options.explanation: Correct. Summarising text you supply is a core strength, and it is easy to check against the thread.

options.text: Deciding which job applicants to reject
options.explanation: Decisions about people carry bias risks and UK GDPR rules on automated decision-making.

options.text: Telling you today's interest rate without web search
options.explanation: Without search, the training cutoff means it can't know current figures.

options.text: Writing very long prompts to get better answers
options.explanation: That's just a long prompt. Prompt injection is an attack.

options.text: Hidden instructions inside content the AI reads, such as an email or web page, trying to make it ignore its rules or do something harmful
options.explanation: Correct. This is why agents that read external content shouldn't be able to send, pay or delete without approval.

options.text: A way to install AI into existing software
options.explanation: That's an integration. Prompt injection is a security risk.

options.text: Retraining a model on new data
options.explanation: That's fine-tuning (lesson 1.2).
